Question 9 of 11 · The Quran

Does the Quran contain knowledge ahead of its time?

The descriptions of nature in the Quran, and the most common objections to them.

The case

01

The Quran describes the embryo's development in stages — confirmed by modern embryology only in the 20th century. What do you make of that?

"We created man from an extract of clay, then made him a drop in a firm resting place, then We made the drop into a clinging form..." — Quran 23:12-14

What does modern science say?

Professor Keith Moore, one of the world's leading embryologists, stated that the Quran's description of embryonic development could not have been known in the 7th century and aligns remarkably with modern findings.

StudyPeer-reviewed: Human Embryology and the Holy Quran (PMC)↗(opens in a new tab)
Read more

The Quran uses 'Alaqah' to describe the early embryo — meaning both 'clinging thing' and 'leech-like'. Under a microscope, the early embryo appears leech-like and clings to the uterine wall. This wasn't in any prior text.

02

Embryology isn't the only example.

The Quran contains several other statements that align with discoveries made centuries later.

More scientific references in the Quran

The Quran states: 'And the heaven We constructed with strength, and indeed, We are its expander.' (51:47). The Arabic word 'mūsiʿūn' means 'we are expanding it' — a direct statement of an expanding universe, 1,300 years before Hubble's 1929 discovery.

Read more

Georges Lemaître proposed the expanding universe in 1927, and Edwin Hubble confirmed it observationally in 1929. The Quran made this statement in 610 AD. No ancient text — Greek, Roman, Persian, or otherwise — contains a comparable claim.

The Quran describes iron as having been 'sent down': 'We sent down iron, in which there is great might.' (57:25). Modern science confirms that iron is not native to Earth — it was forged in dying stars and delivered by meteorite impacts billions of years ago.

Read more

Earth's core is rich in iron, but iron cannot form on a planet — it requires the extreme pressures and temperatures of a supernova. The word 'anzalnā' (sent down) in Arabic is the same word used for rain and other things that come from outside. This was not known until the 20th century.

Objections, answered

The strongest pushback we hear, and our answer to each.

You might say“Could it be a general description anyone might guess?”

Our answer

It's not a general description.

Why it's specific

The Quran uses specific Arabic terms — 'Alaqah' (leech-like clinging form) and 'Mudghah' (chewed-like substance) — matching the exact appearance of the embryo under a microscope at specific stages. These are precise descriptions confirmed 1300 years later.

You might say“He could have guessed or borrowed the knowledge”

Our answer

Could he have borrowed the knowledge?

Why borrowing doesn't explain it

The scientific knowledge in the Quran — embryology, cosmology, oceanography — wasn't available in any text of the 7th century, in any language. Greek texts of the time actually contained errors the Quran doesn't share.

Muhammad ﷺ had no contact with scientists, no access to libraries, and lived in a region with no tradition of scientific inquiry.

You might say“Coincidences happen”

Our answer

Coincidence becomes increasingly unlikely.

The scale of the claim

A single accurate statement could be coincidence. But the Quran contains dozens of precise statements across astronomy, embryology, geology, and oceanography — none contradicted by modern science, all recorded 1400 years ago.
